newsitem.title: FRANCE: France faces cliffhanger vote for change.
newsitem.headline: France faces cliffhanger vote for change.

text.p: Is France becoming ungovernable?
President Jacques Chirac has raised that spectre ahead of Sunday's decisive second round of a parliamentary election that could leave him the prisoner of a hostile, left-wing government.

Some 39 million voters must choose between the ruling centre-right coalition, stripped of unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, and a left-wing alliance whom few political analysts gave the remotest chance of winning just a month ago.

Whoever succeeds in the runoff -- last Sunday's first round gave the combined left a slight advantage -- France is set to have its sixth new prime minister in as many years, a turnover approaching Italy's level of political instability.

If the right snatches victory from the jaws of defeat, Chirac would name popular social Gaullist Philippe Seguin, a nationalist who advocates a strong, protective state, to replace Juppe, in office since May 1995.

Seguin, 54, anointed by the president on Wednesday in a last-ditch bid to rescue the coalition from disarray, has had no time to say how, if at all, he would change policy from Juppe's record of austerity to qualify for a planned single European Union currency.

If the left converts last Sunday's lead in the popular vote into a majority of seats, the prime minister would be Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, a supporter of the euro currency forced to govern in alliance with a Communist party which opposes EU monetary union.
Jospin reasserted in an interview on Thursday that the Socialists' backing for the single currency would prevail.
"One can be against the euro, it's a respectable position, but it will not be the government line," he said.

Faced with the risk of "cohabitation" with the left, Chirac warned on Wednesday that the country would be weakened if the electorate switched sides yet again just two years after choosing him to succeed Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
"France cannot afford to change direction all the time without taking serious risks," he told cabinet ministers.
If the left wins, chances are that Chirac would look for a propitious moment and use his constitutional right to dissolve parliament within a couple of years to seek a new conservative majority.
That could mean yet another change of direction, although the two sides' economic policies are much less far apart today than they were in the more ideological 1970s and early 1980s.

Opinion polls are banned by law between the two rounds, but rumours of unpublished polls favourable to the left caused the Paris Bourse to fall by 3.61 percent on Wednesday and briefly brought the franc under pressure.
Stocks rallied and the franc rose against the mark on Thursday, largely due to a row between the German government and its central bank, the Bundesbank, over accountancy rules for EU monetary union.
While the main French parties differ little on European issues, they do differ on economic and social policy, although Seguin's past views are closer to the Socialists than to Juppe.

The left says it would halt privatisations, although Jospin has given himself a possible let-out on the lucrative sale of a minority state in France Telecom, and create 700,000 youth jobs over three years, half of them in the public sector.
It has also pledged to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay to help combat a record unemployment rate of 12.8 percent during a five-year term.
The centre-right has promised to speed up privatisation and cut taxes to promote private initiative and job-creation.
If the right wins, the sale of a 30-percent stake in France Telecom is due to go ahead in June, as is the sell-off of defence electronics group Thomson CSF.
Juppe spoke last week of the possibility of privatising both state airline Air France, dogged by endemic labour unrest, and long troubled bank Credit Lyonnais this year.

Sunday's result may hinge on two factors -- how the nearly 15 percent of voters who backed the extreme-right National Front in the first round switch their ballots, and who manages to mobilise more of the 32 percent of the electorate who abstained last Sunday.

National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen was due to give his voting recommendations for the runoff at a Paris rally on Thursday night, but his hatred of Chirac means he is unlikely to urge a vote for the centre-right, even with the prospect of the more Eurosceptical Seguin as prime minister.

However the mainstream conservatives are making an all-out bid to win back voters from the extreme-right, giving a prominent last-minute campaign role to hardline former interior minister Charles Pasqua, author of tough 1993 nationality laws.
